print_media.caption: Printer, 3D printer, projector
print_media.description: Printer-scanner, 3D printer, projector with a screen and an interactive panel: output to paper, to plastic and to the big screen.

network.name: Network corner
network.caption: Router, switch, rack
network.description: Switches and patch cables in the server rack; on the table a router, switch, fibre modem, access point, network card, Wi-Fi adapter and NAS. This is how the internet reaches a building.

power.name: Power & cables
power.caption: UPS, cables, hubs
power.description: An uninterruptible power supply (UPS), a docking station, a USB hub and a card reader. HDMI, DisplayPort, USB-C, USB-A and audio cables hang on the wall.

mobile.name: Mobile devices
mobile.caption: Laptop, smartphone, tablet
mobile.description: Laptop, smartphone, tablet, all-in-one, smartwatch and a single-board computer: computers built into one body.

showcase.name: Showcase
showcase.caption: The best of the catalog
showcase.description: In the middle of the hall, a premium case on a turntable, with a monitor, gaming chair, keyboard and headset from the Setup Studio catalog around it.

cpu.adult: Executes instructions: cores and threads, clock speed (GHz), L1–L3 cache, TDP, socket (AM5, LGA1700/1851). F-series chips have no integrated graphics, so a graphics card is required.
cpu.use: In every computer, laptop and smartphone: running programs, calculations, game logic, video encoding.

cooler_air.adult: Heat pipes carry heat from the base to the fin stack and the fan blows it away. What matters: TDP rating, height (case clearance), mounting bracket, 4-pin PWM.
cooler_air.use: In most home and school PCs: quiet, affordable and reliable cooling.

motherboard.adult: Chipset, VRM power stages, DIMM slots, PCIe x16/x1, M.2, SATA, front-panel header. Form factors: ATX, mATX, Mini-ITX; the socket and memory type (DDR4/DDR5) must match the CPU.
motherboard.use: The base of every build: choosing parts starts with the motherboard.

ram.adult: DDR4/DDR5 DIMM modules: capacity (GB), speed (MT/s), latency (CL). Two modules run faster in dual channel; DDR4 and DDR5 have different key notches and do not swap.
ram.use: Browser tabs, games, video editing and programming tools all use a lot of memory.

gpu.adult: Graphics processor and video memory (VRAM), PCIe x16 bus, extra power (8-pin or 12V-2x6), HDMI/DisplayPort outputs. The monitor plugs into the graphics card.
gpu.use: Games, 3D modelling, video editing, training AI models.

psu.adult: Turns 230 V AC into 12/5/3.3 V DC. What matters: wattage, 80 PLUS efficiency, modular cables, the ATX 3.x standard.
psu.use: In every system unit. If it is too weak, the PC shuts down under heavy load.

case_fan.adult: 120/140 mm, speed (RPM), PWM (4-pin) or voltage (3-pin) control; static pressure vs airflow. Front fans take air in, rear and top fans push it out.
case_fan.use: Air exchange inside the case: the CPU and graphics card get cool air.

hdd_35.adult: Magnetic platters, read/write head, actuator; 5400/7200 rpm, about 150–250 MB/s. Cheap per TB, but shock-sensitive and slower than an SSD.
hdd_35.use: Photo and video archives, backups, CCTV recordings, NAS.

ssd_nvme.adult: PCIe 3.0/4.0/5.0 ×4, 3500–14000 MB/s, M.2 2280, M-key. Speed depends on the controller and NAND; not every M.2 slot is NVMe, so check the board.
ssd_nvme.use: System drive: Windows boots in seconds, games and programs open fast.

monitor.adult: Diagonal, resolution, refresh rate (Hz), panel type (IPS/VA/OLED), response time, HDR, inputs (HDMI, DisplayPort, USB-C).
monitor.use: Study, work, design (colour accuracy), esports (144–360 Hz).

keyboard.adult: Membrane vs mechanical switches, layouts (ANSI/ISO, KZ/RU), size (full, TKL, 75 %), connection (wired, 2.4 GHz, Bluetooth), polling rate.

mouse.adult: Optical sensor, DPI (sensitivity), polling rate (Hz), weight, wired or 2.4 GHz / Bluetooth receiver.
mouse.use: Pointing, drawing, design, aiming in games.

microphone.adult: Dynamic or condenser capsule, polar pattern, USB (digital) or XLR/3.5 mm (analogue), sample rate.
microphone.use: Online lessons, podcasts, streaming, voice recording.

webcam.adult: Resolution (1080p/4K), frame rate (30/60 fps), field of view, privacy shutter, built-in mic.

speakers.adult: 2.0 or 2.1 (with subwoofer), power (W RMS), frequency range, active vs passive, 3.5 mm or Bluetooth.
speakers.use: Playing videos in class, music, films, games.

headset.adult: Closed or open-back, drivers, impedance (ohms), microphone; 3.5 mm TRRS, USB or 2.4 GHz wireless.
headset.use: Online lessons, language learning, team chat in games.

printer_inkjet.adult: The print head sprays ink droplets; cartridges or an ink tank, resolution (dpi), CMYK colours.
printer_inkjet.use: Photos, colour posters, documents at home.

cooler_liquid.name: AIO liquid cooler
cooler_liquid.student: Liquid carries the processor’s heat to a radiator, where fans cool it down.
cooler_liquid.purpose: To cool a powerful CPU quietly and efficiently.
cooler_liquid.adult: Closed loop: pump block → tubes → 240/360 mm radiator → 2–3 fans. The pump connects to CPU_FAN/PUMP; the radiator mounts at the top or front of the case.
cooler_liquid.use: Gaming and workstation PCs, showcase builds with glass cases.

mount.label: Mounting
mount.value: Top or front of the case

q1.question: What carries the heat in an AIO cooler?
q1.explain: The pump circulates liquid that carries heat from the CPU to the radiator.

q2.question: How many 120 mm fans fit on a 360 mm radiator?
q2.explain: 360 ÷ 120 = 3. A longer radiator removes more heat.

q3.question: Which header does the pump plug into?
q3.explain: The board controls the pump through the CPU_FAN or PUMP header.

case.name: PC case
case.student: The “house” for every part of the computer: it protects them from dust and knocks.
case.purpose: To hold the parts, organise airflow and provide front-panel ports.
case.adult: Form factors: ATX mid-tower, mATX, Mini-ITX. What matters: airflow (in at the front, out at the back and top), dust filters, clearance for GPU length and cooler height, front panel (USB, audio).
case.use: Any desktop PC; glass-panel cases show off the build.

airflow.label: Airflow
airflow.value: In at the front → out at the back/top

panel.label: Front panel
panel.value: USB-A, USB-C, 3.5 mm audio, power button

q1.question: How does air usually move through a case?
q1.a: In at the back, out at the front
q1.c: In at the front, out at the back and top
q1.explain: Cool air enters at the front; hot air rises and leaves through the rear and top fans.

q2.question: What should you check in a case for a long graphics card?
q2.explain: The maker lists the longest card that fits, e.g. 360 mm.

q3.question: What are the front-panel USB ports for?
q3.a: To plug in drives and devices conveniently
q3.explain: Front USB ports are wired to an internal board header, so you need not reach round the back.

thermal_paste.name: Thermal paste
thermal_paste.student: A paste that fills tiny gaps between the CPU and the cooler and passes heat well.
thermal_paste.purpose: So heat flows from the CPU to the cooler without a barrier.
thermal_paste.adult: Displaces air (a poor conductor) from the micro-roughness of the metal faces. Thermal conductivity 4–12 W/m·K; a pea-sized drop is enough, more does not help.
thermal_paste.use: When fitting a cooler and replacing it every 2–3 years; when servicing laptops and consoles.

q1.question: Why is thermal paste needed?
q1.a: To push air out of the gaps and pass heat to the cooler
q1.explain: Air conducts heat poorly; the paste fills the micro-gaps.

q2.question: How much paste should you apply?
q2.explain: The cooler’s pressure spreads the drop thinly; too much makes cooling worse.

q3.question: What happens to a CPU without paste?
q3.b: It overheats, throttles or shuts down
q3.explain: Heat cannot reach the cooler, so the CPU protects itself by slowing down (throttling).

internal_cables.name: Internal cables
internal_cables.student: Cables that power the parts and connect them to each other.
internal_cables.purpose: To bring power from the PSU and connect drives to the board.
internal_cables.adult: ATX 24-pin (board), EPS 8-pin (CPU), PCIe 8-pin / 12V-2x6 (GPU), SATA power and data, front-panel and fan cables. Connectors are keyed, so they only fit one way.
internal_cables.use: When building a PC; tidy cable management improves airflow.

q1.question: Which cable is the board’s main power?
q1.explain: The 24-pin ATX cable feeds 12/5/3.3 V to the board.

q2.question: Which cable powers the CPU?
q2.explain: The CPU is fed through the EPS 8-pin header at the top corner of the board.

q3.question: Why can’t a connector go in the wrong way?
q3.a: They are keyed (a notch or tab)
q3.explain: The key lets a plug go in only one way, so nothing gets damaged.

cmos_battery.name: CMOS battery
cmos_battery.student: A small battery that keeps the clock and settings while the PC is off.
cmos_battery.purpose: So the UEFI (BIOS) settings and time are not lost.
cmos_battery.adult: A CR2032 lithium cell (3 V) powers the real-time clock (RTC) and UEFI settings; lasts 3–10 years. When it dies, the time and settings reset at every power-on.
cmos_battery.use: On every motherboard; if an old PC loses the time, the battery is the first thing to replace.

q1.question: What happens when the CMOS battery dies?
q1.c: The clock and settings reset at every power-on
q1.explain: The battery powers the RTC clock and UEFI settings when unplugged.

q2.question: Which battery is usually on the board?
q2.explain: A CR2032 is a 3 V lithium cell, 20 mm across and 3.2 mm thick.

q3.question: What is UEFI (BIOS)?
q3.b: Firmware that runs first when the PC starts
q3.explain: UEFI checks the hardware and loads the OS; its settings live in CMOS memory.

hdd_25.name: 2.5″ hard disk
hdd_25.student: A smaller hard disk for laptops: it stores data on a spinning magnetic platter.
hdd_25.purpose: To store lots of data cheaply in laptops and external drives.
hdd_25.adult: 2.5″ form factor, 7–9.5 mm thick, 5400 rpm, SATA. Lighter and more frugal than 3.5″ but slower; in laptops it has been replaced by SSDs.
hdd_25.use: External USB drives, older laptops, game consoles.

q1.question: How does a 2.5″ HDD differ from a 3.5″ one?
q1.explain: It still has a spinning platter inside, just smaller.

q2.question: Where are 2.5″ HDDs used most?
q2.b: In external drives and older laptops
q2.explain: Its small size and USB power suit portable drives.

q3.question: Why must you not drop a hard disk?
q3.c: The head can strike the spinning platter and destroy data
q3.explain: The head flies nanometres above the platter; a knock makes it touch the surface.

ssd_sata.name: SATA SSD (2.5″)
ssd_sata.student: A fast drive with no moving parts: it stores data in flash memory chips.
ssd_sata.purpose: To speed up an older PC: Windows and programs open quickly.
ssd_sata.adult: NAND flash + controller in a 2.5″ shell. The SATA III interface caps it at ≈ 550–560 MB/s: slower than NVMe but 3–5× faster than an HDD; fits any PC with SATA.
ssd_sata.use: Upgrading old PCs and laptops, a second drive, a game library.

q1.question: Why is a SATA SSD faster than an HDD?
q1.b: No mechanics: data is read from flash at once
q1.explain: An SSD has no head or platter, so access takes microseconds.

q2.question: What limits a SATA SSD’s speed?
q2.explain: The NAND could go faster, but SATA tops out at 6 Gbit/s.

q3.question: Which cables does a SATA SSD need?
q3.explain: The data cable goes to the board, the power cable to the PSU.

usb_flash.name: USB flash drive
usb_flash.student: A pocket-sized drive that carries files between computers over USB.
usb_flash.purpose: To carry files, bring a presentation to class, install Windows.
usb_flash.adult: NAND + USB controller; USB 2.0 (≈ 30 MB/s) or USB 3.x (100–400 MB/s). File system FAT32 (files ≤ 4 GB) or exFAT. Use “safely remove” before pulling it out.
usb_flash.use: Handing in schoolwork, bootable installers, moving data.

q1.question: Why is a USB 3.x stick faster than USB 2.0?
q1.explain: USB 2.0 is 480 Mbit/s, USB 3.2 Gen 1 is 5 Gbit/s: almost ten times more.

q2.question: Why can’t a 6 GB file go on a FAT32 stick?
q2.a: FAT32 limits one file to 4 GB
q2.explain: exFAT or NTFS allow large files.

q3.question: What should you do before pulling out a stick?
q3.explain: If a write has not finished, files can be corrupted.

sd_card.name: SD / microSD card
sd_card.student: A tiny memory card for cameras and phones.
sd_card.purpose: To store photos, videos and files in small devices.
sd_card.adult: Formats SD/SDHC (≤ 32 GB)/SDXC (≤ 2 TB), microSD + adapter. Speed classes: U1/U3, V30 (for 4K video), A1/A2 (apps on phones).
sd_card.use: Cameras, action cams, drones, Raspberry Pi, Nintendo Switch.

speed.label: Speed mark
speed.value: U3 / V30 — at least 30 MB/s writes

q1.question: What does “V30” on a card mean?
q1.a: Writes at least 30 MB/s (fine for 4K video)
q1.explain: The V class is the minimum sustained video write speed.

q2.question: How do you use a microSD card in a full SD slot?
q2.explain: The adapter gives microSD the SD shape; the contacts are the same.

q3.question: Where are SD cards used most?
q3.explain: Being tiny and light makes it ideal for cameras.

external_drive.name: External drive
external_drive.student: A drive in a box that plugs in over USB for backups and carrying big files.
external_drive.purpose: To back up data and move lots of files.
external_drive.adult: A 2.5″ HDD or SSD in a USB enclosure, USB 3.2 / USB-C, powered over USB. The 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies of your data, on 2 kinds of media, 1 kept elsewhere.
external_drive.use: Backups, photo/video archives, moving games to a console.

q1.question: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule ask for?
q1.explain: Even if a device fails or a fire happens, the data survives.

q2.question: Where does an external drive usually get power?
q2.explain: 2.5″ drives run on USB’s 5 V.

q3.question: Why is an external SSD better than an external HDD?
q3.explain: An SSD has no moving parts, though a TB still costs more.

optical_disc.name: Optical disc (CD/DVD/Blu-ray)
optical_disc.student: A shiny disc read by a laser: it holds music, films or software.
optical_disc.purpose: To keep and distribute data (music, films, games).
optical_disc.adult: Data is stored as pits and lands along a spiral track. CD 700 MB (780 nm laser), DVD 4.7/8.5 GB (650 nm), Blu-ray 25–100 GB (405 nm blue laser): a shorter wavelength packs data more densely.
optical_disc.use: Archives, films, game consoles, music collections.

q1.question: Why does a Blu-ray hold more than a DVD?
q1.c: The blue laser’s shorter wavelength makes smaller, denser pits
q1.explain: Both are 12 cm across; density depends on the laser.

q2.question: How much data fits on a regular CD?
q2.explain: A CD holds about 700 MB or 80 minutes of audio.

q3.question: What reads the data on a disc?
q3.explain: The laser reflects differently from pits and lands: that is 0 and 1.

optical_drive.name: Optical drive
optical_drive.student: A device that reads and writes CD, DVD or Blu-ray discs.
optical_drive.purpose: To install software from discs, watch films and burn data.
optical_drive.adult: Fits a 5.25″ bay and connects over SATA; laser unit, tray, motor. External USB versions exist. Modern cases and laptops usually lack one, since software is downloaded.
optical_drive.use: Copying data from old discs, archiving, libraries.

q1.question: Why do modern PCs rarely have an optical drive?
q1.explain: USB sticks, the cloud and the internet replaced discs.

q2.question: How does an internal optical drive connect to the board?
q2.explain: Data over a SATA cable, power over SATA power.

q3.question: What is the difference between reading and writing in a drive?
q3.b: Writing uses a stronger laser that leaves marks on the disc
q3.c: Only coloured discs can be written
q3.explain: The laser heats the recording layer; when reading, a weak laser only measures reflection.

graphics_tablet.name: Graphics tablet
graphics_tablet.student: A board with a special pen for drawing on the computer as on paper.
graphics_tablet.purpose: Digital drawing, design and handwritten notes.
graphics_tablet.adult: An electromagnetic (EMR) pen needs no battery; 4096–8192 pressure levels, active area (inches), screen and screenless models; USB-C or Bluetooth.
graphics_tablet.use: Artists, animators, designers and teachers writing formulas in online lessons.

q1.question: What do a tablet’s pressure levels give you?
q1.b: Press harder for a thicker line, lighter for a thinner one
q1.explain: More levels mean finer pressure control.

q2.question: Who uses a graphics tablet most?
q2.explain: Drawing with a pen is far more precise and natural than with a mouse.

q3.question: Why does an EMR pen need no battery?
q3.c: The tablet’s electromagnetic field powers it
q3.explain: The board emits a field; the pen draws energy from it and reports its position.

gamepad.name: Gamepad
gamepad.student: A two-handed controller for playing games.
gamepad.purpose: To control characters and vehicles in games comfortably.
gamepad.adult: Two analogue sticks, analogue triggers (they measure how far you press), rumble motors, XInput; USB-C, 2.4 GHz or Bluetooth, rechargeable battery.
gamepad.use: PC and console games, racing and sports titles.

q1.question: How does an analogue stick differ from a button?
q1.c: It gives direction and amount, not just on/off
q1.explain: Tilt a little to walk slowly, all the way to run.

q2.question: What makes a gamepad vibrate?
q2.explain: An off-centre weight on the motor shaft spins and shakes the pad.

q3.question: How does a wireless gamepad connect to a PC?
q3.a: Via Bluetooth or a 2.4 GHz receiver
q3.explain: A 2.4 GHz receiver usually has lower lag than Bluetooth.

printer_laser.name: Laser printer
printer_laser.student: A printer that prints pages fast by fusing toner powder onto paper.
printer_laser.purpose: To print many documents quickly and cheaply at school and in offices.
printer_laser.adult: The laser draws a charge image on the drum, toner sticks to it and transfers to paper, and the fuser melts it at 180–200 °C. 20–40 pages per minute, duplex, Wi-Fi/Ethernet.
printer_laser.use: Schools, offices, libraries: tests, reports, documents.

q1.question: What does a laser printer print with?
q1.explain: Toner is a powder of plastic and pigment that the fuser melts onto paper.

q2.question: Why does a laser printer suit a school?
q2.explain: One cartridge lasts thousands of pages and never dries out.

q3.question: What does the fuser do?
q3.c: Heats the toner to fix it to the paper
q3.explain: That is why a freshly printed page is warm.

scanner.name: Scanner
scanner.student: A device that copies a paper document or photo into the computer.
scanner.purpose: To digitise, archive and recognise text in documents.
scanner.adult: Flatbed scanner: a CIS/CCD bar under the glass reads the page line by line; 600–4800 dpi; OCR turns text in the image into editable text; ADF feeds pages automatically.
scanner.use: Document archives, digitising old photos, libraries.

q1.question: What does OCR do?
q1.b: Turns scanned text into editable text
q1.explain: Optical Character Recognition reads letters from an image.

q2.question: What is the difference between 300 and 1200 dpi?
q2.c: Dots per inch: 1200 dpi shows more detail
q2.explain: 300 dpi suits documents; photos need 600–1200 dpi.

q3.question: What is an ADF?
q3.a: An automatic feeder for one page after another
q3.explain: An ADF scans dozens of pages without changing them by hand.

projector.name: Projector
projector.student: A device that shows the computer’s picture large on a wall or screen.
projector.purpose: To show slides and videos to the whole class at once.
projector.adult: DLP or LCD, brightness (lumens; 3000+ for a classroom), native resolution (1080p), throw ratio (distance to the screen), keystone correction. Connects over HDMI.

q1.question: What is a projector’s brightness measured in?
q1.explain: A bright classroom needs at least 3000 lumens.

q2.question: How do you connect a laptop to a projector?
q2.explain: HDMI carries video and sound in one cable.

q3.question: What is keystone correction for?
q3.b: To keep the picture rectangular when the projector is tilted
q3.explain: Projecting upwards makes a trapezoid; keystone squares it up.

printer_3d.name: 3D printer
printer_3d.student: A printer that makes real objects from plastic, layer by layer.
printer_3d.purpose: To make prototypes, teaching models and spare parts.
printer_3d.adult: FDM: the extruder melts plastic filament (PLA, PETG) at 200–240 °C, the 0.4 mm nozzle moves in X/Y and the bed steps down in Z; layers are 0.1–0.3 mm. A slicer turns the model into G-code.
printer_3d.use: School robotics, engineering prototypes, medicine, spare parts.

q1.question: How does an FDM printer make an object?
q1.a: It lays melted plastic layer by layer
q1.explain: Each layer sits on the one before: additive manufacturing.

q2.question: What does a slicer do?
q2.c: Splits the 3D model into layers and writes G-code
q2.explain: G-code is the list of motion commands for the printer.

q3.question: What nozzle temperature does PLA need?
q3.explain: The nozzle is hot: never touch it!

interactive_panel.name: Interactive display
interactive_panel.student: A big touchscreen for the classroom that you can write and draw on with a finger.
interactive_panel.purpose: To make lessons visual: board, projector and computer in one.
interactive_panel.adult: A 65–86″ 4K panel, infrared or capacitive touch (20–40 points), built-in Android, an OPS slot for a PC module, HDMI/USB-C inputs, wireless casting from a laptop.
interactive_panel.use: School classrooms, lecture halls, office meetings.

q1.question: How is an interactive display different from a projector?
q1.b: It is a touchscreen that makes its own light
q1.explain: A projector throws light on a screen; the panel is a big monitor you can write on.

q2.question: How does a teacher connect a laptop to the panel?
q2.explain: One USB-C cable can carry video, touch and charging.

q3.question: What is the OPS slot for?
q3.c: To slot a PC module into the panel
q3.explain: OPS is a Windows PC inside the panel: no cables needed.

router.name: Router
router.student: Connects home or school devices to the internet and provides Wi-Fi.
router.purpose: To share one internet connection with every device at home or in class and to provide Wi-Fi.
router.adult: The WAN port goes to the provider (modem); the LAN ports and Wi-Fi form the local network. The router shares one public IP through NAT, hands out addresses with DHCP and filters incoming connections with a firewall. Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax), 2.4 and 5 GHz.
router.use: In every home, school and café: phones, laptops and TVs reach the internet through it.

q1.question: What does a router do with the internet connection?
q1.c: Shares one connection with many devices
q1.explain: Through NAT the router lets every home device share one public address.

q2.question: Which router port goes to the provider (modem)?
q2.explain: WAN is the outside network, LAN the inside one. The WAN port is usually a different colour.

q3.question: What does DHCP in a router do?
q3.explain: Without DHCP you would have to type an IP address into every device by hand.

switch.name: Network switch
switch.student: Joins many computers into one network with cables.
switch.purpose: Building one shared local network for every PC, printer and server in a classroom or office.
switch.adult: A switch works at layer 2 (the OSI data-link layer): it learns which MAC address sits behind each port and sends a frame only to the right port. 1–10 Gbit/s per port; managed models add VLANs, QoS and PoE; SFP+ slots take fibre.
switch.use: Computer classrooms, offices and server racks: every wired device ends up at a switch.

q1.question: How does a switch differ from a router?
q1.a: A switch joins devices inside one network; a router links networks (e.g. to the internet)
q1.explain: A switch is the hub of the local network; a router is its gateway to the outside world.

q2.question: How does a switch know which port to send data to?
q2.c: It always sends to every port
q2.explain: The switch remembers the sender of every frame and later sends data only to that port.

q3.question: What do you need to cable 25 classroom computers into one network?
q3.explain: Each computer gets its own cable to a switch port; 48 ports leave room to spare for 25 devices.

modem.name: Modem
modem.student: Turns the provider’s signal (fibre, DSL) into one computers understand.
modem.purpose: Letting the internet into a building: the bridge between the provider and the home network.
modem.adult: “Modem” = modulator–demodulator. On fibre it is an ONT (GPON terminal) that turns light pulses into an electrical signal at 1–2.5 Gbit/s. A DSL modem works over the phone line (RJ-11). Provider boxes often combine modem, router and Wi-Fi in one case.
modem.use: It sits where the internet enters a home or school; the router plugs in after it.

q1.question: What does the word “modem” stand for?
q1.explain: A modem modulates the signal it sends down the line and demodulates the one it receives.

q2.question: What is the box that converts the light signal on fibre internet called?
q2.explain: An ONT takes the provider’s fibre and gives you an Ethernet port: it is a fibre modem.

q3.question: Can a modem and a router be in one box?
q3.a: Yes, most provider devices are like that
q3.explain: Such an all-in-one box does the job of the modem, router and Wi-Fi point together.

wifi_adapter.name: Wi-Fi adapter
wifi_adapter.student: Gives a computer without Wi-Fi a wireless connection.
wifi_adapter.purpose: Getting a PC online without a cable, or swapping old Wi-Fi for a faster standard.
wifi_adapter.adult: Comes as USB (a tiny dongle or one with an antenna) or a PCIe x1 card. Standards: Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac) or Wi-Fi 6/6E (802.11ax) on 2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz. 2.4 GHz reaches further but is slower and busier; 5 GHz is faster but passes walls poorly. External antennas improve reception.
wifi_adapter.use: Getting an old or desktop PC online without running a cable.

q1.question: When do you need a Wi-Fi adapter?
q1.c: When the computer has no built-in Wi-Fi
q1.explain: Laptops usually have Wi-Fi but many desktops do not; an adapter fills the gap.

q2.question: Which band is faster but has a shorter range?
q2.explain: Higher frequency means more speed but weaker penetration through walls.

q3.question: What do a Wi-Fi adapter’s external antennas give you?
q3.explain: Larger antennas catch weak signals better, especially in a room far from the router.

nic.name: Network card
nic.student: Connects a computer to the network over Ethernet.
nic.purpose: A steady, fast, low-latency wired connection.
nic.adult: A network card (NIC) splits data into frames and sends them down the cable as electrical signals. Every card has a unique 48-bit MAC address from the factory. Motherboards carry a built-in 1–2.5 Gbit/s chip; an add-in PCIe card gives 10 Gbit/s or SFP+ fibre.
nic.use: A wired link is steadier and faster: gaming, servers, classroom PCs.

q1.question: What does every network card have that is unique?
q1.explain: The MAC address is set at the factory; switches tell devices apart by it.

q2.question: Where does an add-in network card go in a desktop PC?
q2.a: Into a PCIe slot on the motherboard
q2.explain: A network card is an expansion card; it goes into a PCIe x1 or x4 slot.

q3.question: How do most modern motherboards handle networking?
q3.c: A network chip is built in, with RJ-45 on the rear panel
q3.explain: An add-in card is only needed for more speed (10 Gbit/s) or fibre.

ethernet_cable.name: Ethernet cable
ethernet_cable.student: A cable with RJ-45 plugs that links network devices.
ethernet_cable.purpose: To link network devices (PC, router, switch) with a reliable wired connection.
ethernet_cable.adult: Inside are 4 twisted pairs (8 wires) with RJ-45 (8P8C) plugs on the ends. Categories: Cat5e 1 Gbit/s, Cat6 10 Gbit/s up to 55 m, Cat6a 10 Gbit/s up to 100 m. One run may be at most 100 m long. Twisting cuts interference between pairs (crosstalk); wires are crimped in T568B order.
ethernet_cable.use: From every classroom PC to the switch, from router to modem, between servers.

q1.question: How long can a single Ethernet run be?
q1.explain: Beyond 100 m the signal fades: put a switch in between or use fibre.

q2.question: Why are the wires twisted in pairs?
q2.explain: Outside noise hits both wires of a pair equally and cancels out.

q3.question: Which category carries 10 Gbit/s up to 100 m?
q3.explain: Cat6a is better shielded; Cat6 holds 10 Gbit/s only up to 55 m.

access_point.name: Access point
access_point.student: Extends Wi-Fi coverage in a large building.
access_point.purpose: Removing Wi-Fi dead spots in corridors and classrooms and serving many students at once.
access_point.adult: An access point (AP) turns the wired network into a wireless one but does no NAT/DHCP like a router. It mounts on a ceiling or wall and takes power over PoE through the same Ethernet cable. Several APs with one network name (SSID) hand a device from room to room without a drop (roaming). Wi-Fi 6/6E, 100+ clients.
access_point.use: Schools, universities, offices and airports: one AP in every corridor.

q1.question: Why does a school use several access points instead of one router?
q1.b: To cover the whole building with Wi-Fi
q1.explain: One device’s signal fades through walls and floors; every area needs its own AP.

q2.question: What is PoE?
q2.a: Power over Ethernet: data and power through one cable
q2.explain: PoE means no separate socket at the ceiling: the switch supplies the power.

q3.question: Where is an access point usually mounted?
q3.c: On the ceiling or high on a wall
q3.explain: Up high, furniture and people block the signal less.

nas.name: Network storage (NAS)
nas.student: A “home cloud” that stores shared files for every device on the network.
nas.purpose: Keeping a family’s or class’s photos, documents and backups in one place on its own network.
nas.adult: A NAS is a small computer with its own CPU and OS and 2–4 drive bays. Files are reached over the network (SMB, web, app). RAID 1 writes every file to two drives at once, so data survives if one fails. RAID is not a backup, though: a file deleted by mistake or encrypted by ransomware is gone from both drives.
nas.use: A family photo archive, shared school folders, CCTV recordings.

q1.question: What does RAID 1 do in a NAS?
q1.a: Writes an identical copy of every file to a second drive
q1.explain: The two drives mirror each other: if one dies, the other still has everything.

q2.question: How do computers reach the files on a NAS?
q2.explain: The NAS is cabled to the network, and its files show up on every computer as a network drive.

q3.question: Does RAID replace a backup?
q3.b: No, you still need a separate backup
q3.explain: A deleted or ransomware-encrypted file vanishes from both drives; a backup must live elsewhere.

server_rack.name: Server rack
server_rack.student: A cabinet that holds servers and network gear in order.
server_rack.purpose: To keep servers, switches, UPS units and cables in one place, tidy, secure and cool.
server_rack.adult: The standard width is 19 inches and height is counted in units: 1U = 44.45 mm, racks are 22U–42U. Inside: a patch panel (every cable ends neatly in one place), switches, servers, a PDU (power strip) and a UPS. Air enters at the front and leaves at the back; doors are vented and cables run through organisers.
server_rack.use: School server rooms, offices, data centres.

q1.question: What does “1U” mean in a rack?
q1.explain: Device heights are given in units: a 1U switch, a 2U server and so on.

q2.question: What is the standard width of a server rack?
q2.explain: The 19-inch standard lets gear from any maker fit the same rack.

q3.question: What is a patch panel for?
q3.a: To end every cable neatly in one place
q3.explain: Cables from the rooms are fixed to the panel; short patch cords run to the switch.

ups.name: Uninterruptible power supply (UPS)
ups.student: Keeps the computer running on a battery during a power cut so you can save your work.
ups.purpose: Not losing data in a sudden power cut, and protecting equipment from voltage spikes.
ups.adult: Rated in VA and W (e.g. 1500 VA / 900 W). Line-interactive units correct low or high voltage (AVR); online units always feed the load through the battery. A 12 V lead-acid battery keeps a PC going 5–15 minutes, enough to save work and shut down properly. Over USB the computer shuts itself down when the charge runs low.
ups.use: School servers, network cabinets, tills, medical and home computers.

q1.question: What does a UPS do during a power cut?
q1.a: Turns the PC off at once
q1.b: Runs the PC from its battery for a few minutes
q1.explain: The switch-over takes milliseconds, so the computer stays on.

q2.question: How long does a home UPS usually keep a PC running?
q2.a: 5–15 minutes: enough to save work and shut down properly
q2.explain: A UPS is not a generator; its job is to give you time to shut down safely without losing data.

q3.question: Why connect a UPS to the computer over USB?
q3.c: So the PC shuts down properly by itself when the battery runs low
q3.explain: Even with no one around (at night) the server saves its data and shuts down in order.

docking_station.name: Docking station
docking_station.student: Connects a monitor, keyboard, network and charging to a laptop through one cable.
docking_station.purpose: Turning a laptop into a full workstation in one move and solving the shortage of ports.
docking_station.adult: It links to the laptop over USB-C or Thunderbolt 4 (40 Gbit/s). Inside are a USB hub, video outputs (HDMI, DisplayPort: two 4K monitors), a network chip (RJ-45) and audio. With Power Delivery (PD) it charges the laptop through the same cable at up to 90–100 W; the dock has its own power brick.
docking_station.use: In offices and on teachers’ desks: one cable turns a laptop into a full workstation.

q1.question: What is the main benefit of a docking station?
q1.c: One cable connects the laptop to everything on the desk
q1.explain: Monitors, keyboard, network and charger stay plugged into the dock; only one cable goes to the laptop.

q2.question: What is Power Delivery (PD)?
q2.a: Charging the laptop through the same USB-C cable
q2.explain: With PD the devices negotiate and raise the voltage from 5 V up to 20 V, which carries high power.

q3.question: How does a dock usually connect to the laptop?
q3.explain: A single USB-C/Thunderbolt cable carries data, video and power at once.

usb_hub.name: USB hub
usb_hub.student: Turns one USB port into several.
usb_hub.purpose: Plugging several devices at once into a laptop with few ports.
usb_hub.adult: All hub ports share the bandwidth of one upstream port: 5 Gbit/s in total for USB 3.2 Gen 1. A bus-powered hub suits low-power devices such as mice and sticks; external HDDs need an active hub with its own adapter. USB 3.x sockets usually have a blue insert.
usb_hub.use: Thin laptops with few ports, a student desk full of sticks and peripherals.

q1.question: Does a hub increase the total USB speed?
q1.a: No: all its ports share the speed of one port
q1.explain: Copy to two sticks at once and each gets roughly half the speed.

q2.question: When does a hub need its own power adapter?
q2.c: For power-hungry devices such as an external HDD
q2.explain: One USB port supplies limited current; split among several devices, a drive may fail to spin up.

q3.question: What colour is the plastic inside a USB 3.0 port usually?
q3.explain: Black means USB 2.0, blue USB 3.x; the blue port has extra contacts.

card_reader.name: Card reader
card_reader.student: Lets a computer read SD and microSD cards.
card_reader.purpose: To read and write the memory cards of cameras, drones and phones on a computer.
card_reader.adult: SD and microSD slots, sometimes CFexpress. Card and reader must share the bus standard: UHS-I up to 104 MB/s, UHS-II (a second row of pins) up to 312 MB/s. A UHS-II card in a UHS-I reader runs at UHS-I speed only. It plugs in over USB 3.2; eject the card safely before pulling it out.
card_reader.use: Photographers, video bloggers, writing an OS for a Raspberry Pi, copying files off an old phone.

q1.question: Which cards does a card reader read?
q1.explain: Here “card” means a flash memory card that stores photos and files.

q2.question: Why is a fast UHS-II card slow in a cheap reader?
q2.b: The reader only supports UHS-I, so the card runs at that speed
q2.explain: A chain is as fast as its slowest link: UHS-II needs a UHS-II reader too.

q3.question: What should you do before pulling a card out of the reader?
q3.explain: Pulling it out mid-write can corrupt the files and the file system.

hdmi_cable.name: HDMI cable
hdmi_cable.student: Carries video and sound to a monitor, TV or projector.
hdmi_cable.purpose: Putting a laptop screen on the classroom projector, or a game on the TV.
hdmi_cable.adult: A digital signal (TMDS / FRL). Versions: HDMI 1.4 = 4K 30 Hz, 2.0 = 4K 60 Hz (18 Gbit/s), 2.1 = 4K 120 Hz and 8K 60 Hz (48 Gbit/s, “Ultra High Speed” cable). ARC/eARC sends TV sound back to a soundbar; CEC lets one remote control several devices. 19 pins; plugs A (full), C (mini), D (micro).
hdmi_cable.use: Laptop to projector, games console to TV, PC to monitor.

q1.question: What does an HDMI cable carry?
q1.explain: That is why a TV or projector needs no separate audio cable.

q2.question: Which cable do you need for 4K at 120 Hz?
q2.explain: 4K 120 Hz needs about 40+ Gbit/s; an older cable passes only up to 18 Gbit/s.

q3.question: What does HDMI ARC let you do?
q3.b: Send TV sound back to a soundbar over the same cable
q3.explain: ARC stands for Audio Return Channel.

displayport_cable.name: DisplayPort cable
displayport_cable.student: A cable for high-refresh video to a monitor.
displayport_cable.purpose: Using a gaming monitor’s full refresh rate (144+ Hz) and several monitors.
displayport_cable.adult: A packet-based digital link. DP 1.2 = 21.6 Gbit/s, 1.4 = 32.4 Gbit/s (4K 240 Hz with DSC compression), 2.1 = up to 80 Gbit/s. MST chains several monitors from one port. Adaptive sync (G-Sync, FreeSync) removes tearing. The plug has a latch: press its button to pull it out.
displayport_cable.use: Gaming monitors (144–360 Hz), multi-monitor workstations, graphics cards.

q1.question: Why do gamers prefer DisplayPort?
q1.c: High refresh rates and adaptive sync
q1.explain: Most graphics cards deliver 144–360 Hz and G-Sync/FreeSync first and foremost over DP.

q2.question: What is DisplayPort MST?
q2.a: Chaining several monitors from one port
q2.explain: MST = Multi-Stream Transport: several video streams share one cable.

q3.question: How does a DP plug stay in its socket?
q3.b: With a latch: press its button to release
q3.explain: Do not yank the cable: press the latch button first.

usb_c_cable.name: USB-C cable
usb_c_cable.student: A reversible all-round cable: charging, data and video.
usb_c_cable.purpose: Charging and connecting everything with one cable instead of a different one per device.
usb_c_cable.adult: A symmetrical 24-pin plug that fits either way up. Speed depends on the cable: USB 2.0 480 Mbit/s, USB 3.2 10–20 Gbit/s, USB4 / Thunderbolt 40–80 Gbit/s. Power Delivery: 60 W (3 A), or 100 W / 240 W with an e-marker chip. DisplayPort Alt Mode sends video to a monitor. Cables that look alike can do very different things.
usb_c_cable.use: Charging phones, laptops and tablets; connecting docks, monitors, external SSDs.

q1.question: What is special about the USB-C plug?
q1.explain: The pins are mirrored on both sides, so there is no “right way up”.

q2.question: Are all USB-C cables the same?
q2.c: No: speed, power and video support differ
q2.explain: A cheap cable gives only 480 Mbit/s and 60 W; a monitor or 240 W needs a special one.

q3.question: How can a monitor work over USB-C?
q3.explain: In Alt Mode some of the USB-C lanes carry a DisplayPort signal.

usb_a_cable.name: USB-A cable
usb_a_cable.student: The common cable for mice, keyboards, sticks and more.
usb_a_cable.purpose: Connecting printers, scanners and older devices to a computer.
usb_a_cable.adult: One end is USB-A (the computer side), the other USB-B (printers, scanners), micro-B (older phones) or USB-C. USB 2.0 = 480 Mbit/s, 4 pins; USB 3.x = 5–10 Gbit/s, 9 pins, blue insert. A standard port gives 5 V at 0.5 A (USB 2.0) or 0.9 A (USB 3.0). The A plug is not reversible: it fits one way only.
usb_a_cable.use: Hooking printers and scanners to a PC, charging older devices, peripherals.

q1.question: Where is the squarish USB-B end usually used?
q1.explain: The B end marks the device side and the A end the computer side, so you cannot mix them up.

q2.question: How much power does a standard USB 2.0 port supply?
q2.explain: That is why an external HDD sometimes needs two USB plugs or its own power brick.

q3.question: How can you recognise a USB 3.0 port?
q3.c: A blue insert and extra contacts
q3.explain: Blue is the agreed sign of USB 3.x; you may also see “SS” (SuperSpeed) next to it.

audio_cable.name: Audio cable (3.5 mm)
audio_cable.student: A cable that carries sound to speakers and headphones.
audio_cable.purpose: Sending the computer’s sound to speakers and talking into a microphone.
audio_cable.adult: The 3.5 mm mini-jack. TRS (3 contacts) is stereo: left, right, ground. TRRS (4 contacts) is stereo plus microphone (a headset). The signal is analogue, so long cables can pick up noise. PC colour codes: green = output (speakers, headphones), pink = microphone, blue = line in.
audio_cable.use: Speakers, headphones, headsets, a classroom projector or stereo.

q1.question: Which colour PC jack takes headphones or speakers?
q1.explain: Green is sound out, pink is microphone in, blue is line in.

q2.question: What does a TRRS plug (4 contacts) add to TRS?
q2.explain: Phone headsets carry both sound and the microphone through one plug.

q3.question: What kind of signal does a 3.5 mm cable carry?
q3.explain: The sound card turns digital audio into a voltage wave, which travels down the cable in analogue form.

laptop.name: Laptop
laptop.student: A portable computer with a screen, keyboard and battery.
laptop.purpose: To use a computer anywhere: in class, on the move, at home.
laptop.adult: Every part fits a thin case: a mobile CPU (15–45 W), usually integrated graphics, LPDDR5 memory (often soldered), an M.2 NVMe SSD and a 50–99 Wh lithium-ion battery. Cooling is a heat pipe and a small fan. Upgrades are limited: usually only the SSD, sometimes the memory.
laptop.use: Study, programming, office work, online lessons, travel.

q1.question: Why does a laptop CPU use less power than a desktop one?
q1.a: To save battery and limit heat in a thin case
q1.explain: A thin case cannot fit a big heatsink, so mobile chips are built to be frugal.

q2.question: What does “Wh” on a battery mean?
q2.explain: A 60 Wh battery runs a laptop drawing 10 W for about 6 hours.

q3.question: What can you usually upgrade in a laptop?
q3.c: The SSD, and the memory if it is not soldered
q3.explain: The CPU and graphics are soldered on; the SSD and sometimes the memory sit in slots.

all_in_one.name: All-in-one PC
all_in_one.student: A computer with every part built into the monitor.
all_in_one.purpose: A full computer that takes little desk space and plugs in with one cable.
all_in_one.adult: An all-in-one puts the motherboard, CPU, memory, SSD, speakers and webcam behind the screen. Laptop-class parts are common, since cooling must fit a slim case. External or internal power supply; Wi-Fi/Bluetooth built in. Drawbacks: limited upgrades, and if the screen breaks the whole computer goes in for repair.
all_in_one.use: Libraries, reception desks, school offices, the family computer at home.

q1.question: Where are an all-in-one’s parts?
q1.c: Behind the screen, in one case
q1.explain: Hence “all-in-one”: everything is in one unit.

q2.question: What is an advantage of an all-in-one?
q2.a: Few cables and a tidy, compact desk
q2.b: The graphics card is easy to swap
q2.explain: There are no cables between tower and monitor, just one power cable.

q3.question: What is a drawback of an all-in-one?
q3.b: If the screen breaks, the whole computer goes in for repair
q3.explain: With a normal PC you just swap the monitor; in an all-in-one they cannot be separated.

smartphone.name: Smartphone
smartphone.student: A pocket computer: calls, internet, camera, apps.
smartphone.purpose: Calls, internet, photos, navigation and learning apps: a computer in your pocket.
smartphone.adult: Its heart is an SoC (System on a Chip): ARM CPU, GPU, neural engine (NPU) and cellular modem on one chip. 8–16 GB LPDDR5, UFS 4.0 storage. Sensors: accelerometer, gyroscope, GPS, compass, proximity. A 6–7″ OLED screen at 60–120 Hz, a 4000–5000 mAh battery, fast charging over USB-C.
smartphone.use: Everyday contact, mobile banking, maps, photos and video, learning apps.

q1.question: What is an SoC?
q1.b: A system on a chip: CPU, graphics and modem together
q1.explain: With everything on one chip, the phone stays small and efficient.

q2.question: Which sensor rotates the screen when you turn the phone?
q2.explain: The accelerometer senses which way gravity points; the gyroscope measures rotation.

q3.question: What does “mAh” measure?
q3.explain: A 5000 mAh battery can deliver 500 mA for about 10 hours.

tablet.name: Tablet
tablet.student: A light computer with a big touchscreen.
tablet.purpose: Reading textbooks, taking notes and drawing anywhere, without a laptop.
tablet.adult: Built on a mobile SoC like a phone, but with an 8–13″ screen. You mainly use your fingers; a stylus (an active pen with 4096 pressure levels) and a clip-on keyboard bring it close to a laptop. OS: iPadOS, Android or Windows. A 7000–10000 mAh battery lasts about 10 hours.
tablet.use: E-textbooks, classroom quizzes, drawing, video lessons.

q1.question: What mainly sets a tablet apart from a laptop?
q1.a: It is run mainly by touch; a keyboard is optional
q1.explain: A tablet is a single touchscreen slab; you add a keyboard or pen if you like.

q2.question: What is a stylus for?
q2.c: Writing and drawing precisely on the screen
q2.explain: An active stylus senses pressure, so lines come out as if drawn with a pen.

q3.question: Which of these is NOT a tablet operating system?
q3.explain: BIOS/UEFI is firmware that runs at power-on, not an operating system.

smartwatch.name: Smartwatch
smartwatch.student: A tiny computer on your wrist: notifications, steps, heart rate.
smartwatch.purpose: To show notifications and track activity and health: a tiny computer on your wrist.
smartwatch.adult: A small SoC and a 1.2–2″ AMOLED screen. Green LEDs and a light sensor on the back (PPG) measure your pulse, an accelerometer counts steps, GPS records a run, and some have SpO₂ and ECG. They talk to the phone over Bluetooth Low Energy. Magnetic or wireless charging; the battery lasts 1–14 days.
smartwatch.use: Sport and health, notifications, phone-free payments, GPS watches for children.

q1.question: How does a smartwatch measure your pulse?
q1.b: With green LEDs and a light sensor on the back
q1.c: With a camera on the screen
q1.explain: Each heartbeat makes the blood absorb more light; the sensor counts those changes (PPG).

q2.question: How does a smartwatch usually get notifications?
q2.a: Over Bluetooth from the paired phone
q2.explain: Bluetooth Low Energy uses little power, so the watch battery lasts.

q3.question: How is a smartwatch usually charged?
q3.c: With a magnetic or wireless charger
q3.explain: With no open sockets the case is better protected against water.

sbc.name: Single-board computer (Raspberry Pi)
sbc.student: A whole computer on one small board, for robotics and coding.
sbc.purpose: A cheap, tiny computer for robotics, coding, small servers and smart-home projects.
sbc.adult: Raspberry Pi 5: a 4-core ARM Cortex-A76 (2.4 GHz), 2–16 GB LPDDR4X, the OS on a microSD card (or an NVMe SSD via PCIe). 2 × micro-HDMI (4K), USB 3.0, gigabit Ethernet, Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth 5. A 40-pin GPIO header for LEDs, sensors and motors. Runs Linux (Raspberry Pi OS) and is programmed in Python. Powered over USB-C, 5 V / 5 A.
sbc.use: School robotics, IoT projects, weather stations, media centres, learning Python.

q1.question: Where is a Raspberry Pi’s operating system usually stored?
q1.explain: You write the OS to a microSD on a computer and slot the card in, so switching systems is easy.

q2.question: What are the GPIO pins for?
q2.explain: GPIO = General Purpose Input/Output: a program switches or reads the voltage on a pin.

q3.question: What architecture is the Raspberry Pi’s processor?
q3.explain: ARM draws little power, so the board runs passively or with a tiny fan.

system_unit.title: Taking a system unit apart
system_unit.intro: A technician always takes a computer apart in this order: unplug it, remove the side panel, take out the parts mounted on the board, and the motherboard itself last.

panel.name: Side panel
panel.text: The glass panel keeps dust off the parts. Before removing it, shut the PC down, unplug the power cable and discharge static by touching the metal case.
panel.does: Keeps dust and knocks off the parts
panel.ask: What does the side panel do?

gpu.name: Graphics card
gpu.text: It computes the picture and sends it to the monitor. Unplug its power cable, undo the rear screws, press the PCIe slot latch and pull it out.
gpu.does: Computes the picture and sends it to the monitor
gpu.ask: What does the graphics card do?

ram.name: Memory (RAM)
ram.text: It holds running programs and data for the moment. Open the latches at the ends of the slot and the module pops up.
ram.does: Holds running programs for the moment

cooler.name: CPU cooler
cooler.text: Heat pipes and fins carry the CPU’s heat to the fan. Unplug the fan cable and loosen the mounting screws in a cross pattern.
cooler.does: Carries the heat away from the CPU
cooler.ask: What does the CPU cooler do?

cpu.name: Processor (CPU)
cpu.text: The “brain” that runs every program’s instructions. Lift the socket lever and lift the CPU straight up by its edges; never touch the contacts.

ssd.name: M.2 SSD
ssd.text: The operating system and files live here and survive without power. Undo one screw and slide the module out at 30°.
ssd.does: Stores the system and files for good
ssd.ask: What does the M.2 SSD do?

psu.name: Power supply
psu.text: It turns 230 V AC from the socket into the 12, 5 and 3.3 V DC the parts need. Unplug all its cables and undo the four rear screws.
psu.does: Turns mains power into the voltages the parts need
psu.ask: What does the power supply do?

fans.name: Case fans
fans.text: The front fans pull cool air in; hot air leaves at the back and top. Unplug their cables and undo the screws.
fans.does: Pull cool air into the case
fans.ask: What does the case fans do?

motherboard.name: Motherboard
motherboard.text: The main board that links every part. It comes out last: unplug the 24- and 8-pin cables and front-panel wires, then undo the standoff screws.

laptop.title: Taking a laptop apart
laptop.intro: In a laptop every part is packed tightly into a thin case. Once the bottom cover is off, the battery is disconnected first: that prevents short circuits.

lid.name: Display lid
lid.text: The lid holds the screen, webcam and Wi-Fi antennas. It sits on hinges: open it first and lay the laptop on a soft cloth.
lid.does: Holds the screen, camera and Wi-Fi antennas
lid.ask: What does the display lid do?

bottom_cover.name: Bottom cover
bottom_cover.text: It covers the insides and carries the air vents. Undo 8–10 screws and gently release the clips with a plastic pry tool.
bottom_cover.does: Covers the insides and lets air in
bottom_cover.ask: What does the bottom cover do?

battery.name: Battery
battery.text: The lithium-ion battery runs the laptop for 6–15 hours. It is disconnected first; never puncture a swollen battery.
battery.does: Powers the laptop away from a socket

ssd.name: M.2 SSD
ssd.text: The drive with the system and files. One screw holds it: the easiest part of a laptop to upgrade.
ssd.does: Stores the system and files for good
ssd.ask: What does the M.2 SSD do?

ram.name: Memory (SO-DIMM)
ram.text: The short laptop memory module. Spread the side latches and it tilts up 30°. In thin laptops memory may be soldered to the board.
ram.does: Holds running programs for the moment

wifi.name: Wi-Fi module
wifi.text: An M.2 2230 card for wireless and Bluetooth. First unclip the two antenna leads that run to the antennas in the lid.
wifi.ask: What does the Wi-Fi module do?

display_cable.name: Display cable (eDP)
display_cable.text: A thin cable carries the picture and camera signal from the board to the screen. Pull its connector straight out by the tab.
display_cable.does: Carries the picture from the board to the screen
display_cable.ask: What does the display cable (eDP) do?

speakers.name: Speakers
speakers.text: Two small speakers sit in the front corners and fire downwards. One connector links them to the board.

cooling.name: Cooling
cooling.text: A copper heat pipe carries CPU and GPU heat to a radiator and a small fan blows it out. Renew the thermal paste whenever you remove it.
cooling.does: Moves CPU and graphics heat out of the case

motherboard.name: Motherboard
motherboard.text: In a laptop the CPU and graphics are soldered to the board, so they cannot be swapped on their own. The board comes out last.
motherboard.does: Carries the processor and links every module

smartphone.title: Taking a smartphone apart
smartphone.intro: In a smartphone the parts are held by glue and tiny screws. The SIM tray comes out first, the screen is warmed and lifted with a suction cup, and the battery connector is unplugged first.

sim_tray.name: SIM tray
sim_tray.text: It holds the SIM card that connects the phone to the carrier. Press a pin into the side hole and pull the tray out.
sim_tray.does: Holds the SIM card that links the phone to the carrier
sim_tray.ask: What does the SIM tray do?

display.name: Display
display.text: The OLED panel and touch glass are one module: it shows the picture and senses your finger. Warm the edges, lift with a suction cup and unplug its two cables.
display.does: Shows the picture and senses touch

battery.name: Battery
battery.text: A flat lithium-polymer battery (4000–5000 mAh) powers the phone all day. Pull its stretch-release adhesive tabs; never bend or puncture it.

cameras.name: Cameras
cameras.text: Main, ultra-wide and front cameras, each with a lens, sensor and stabiliser. Unplug their cables and lift them out.

mainboard.name: Mainboard and SoC
mainboard.text: A stacked board: the SoC (CPU, graphics, neural engine and modem on one chip), memory, storage and the Wi-Fi and cellular chips. Undo its screws, unplug every cable and lift it out.
mainboard.does: Does all the computing: the phone’s brain
mainboard.ask: What does the mainboard and SoC do?

speaker.name: Speaker
speaker.text: The bottom speaker plays ringtones and music, the top one is for calls. Undo its screw and lift it by the edge.

vibration.name: Vibration motor
vibration.text: A linear motor shakes a small weight back and forth so you feel notifications. Unplug its cable and peel it off.
vibration.ask: What does the vibration motor do?

tablet.title: Taking a tablet apart
tablet.intro: A tablet is a scaled-up phone: a big screen, a two-cell battery and speakers in the four corners. The screen is warmed and opened all round with thin plastic cards.

display.name: Display
display.text: The 10–13″ touchscreen shows the picture and senses fingers and the stylus. Warm the edges, work round with plastic cards and unplug its cables.
display.does: Shows the picture and senses fingers and stylus

battery.name: Battery
battery.text: The two-cell battery (7000–10000 mAh) is the largest part and gives about 10 hours. Free it from its glue carefully with isopropyl alcohol.
battery.does: Powers the tablet for about 10 hours

cameras.name: Cameras
cameras.text: The rear camera scans documents, the front one is for video calls. Unplug their cables and lift them out.
cameras.does: Scan documents and make video calls

mainboard.name: Mainboard and SoC
mainboard.text: A long narrow board sits between the battery cells: SoC, memory, storage and wireless chips. Undo its screws and unplug its cables.
mainboard.ask: What does the mainboard and SoC do?

speakers.name: Speakers
speakers.text: Four corner speakers give stereo sound whichever way you hold the tablet. One screw holds each.
speakers.does: Give stereo sound in any orientation

usb_port.name: USB-C port board
usb_port.text: The port for charging, data and video output. It sits on its own small board, so a worn port means swapping just that board.
usb_port.does: Provides the charging and data port
usb_port.ask: What does the USB-C port board do?

all_in_one.title: Taking an all-in-one apart
all_in_one.intro: Every part of an all-in-one is behind the screen. Lay it face down on a soft cloth, remove the stand and open the back cover.

stand.name: Stand
stand.text: It holds the screen and sets its tilt. Undo the four screws under the stand cover.
stand.does: Holds the screen and sets its tilt

back_cover.name: Back cover
back_cover.text: A plastic or aluminium cover hides the insides; vents along the top let hot air out. Release its clips all round with a plastic pry tool.
back_cover.does: Covers the insides and lets hot air out
back_cover.ask: What does the back cover do?

speakers.name: Speakers
speakers.text: Two speakers along the bottom edge fire forwards. Unplug the cable and undo the screws.

cooling.name: Cooling
cooling.text: A heat pipe takes the CPU’s heat to a radiator and a blower pushes it out through the top vents. Renew the thermal paste when you remove it.
cooling.does: Moves the CPU’s heat out of the case

ram.name: Memory (SO-DIMM)
ram.text: Short modules as in a laptop; many all-in-ones are upgraded this way. Spread the latches and the module tilts up.
ram.does: Holds running programs for the moment

ssd.name: M.2 SSD
ssd.text: The drive with the system and files. It sits in the board’s M.2 slot under one screw, the easiest part of an all-in-one to upgrade.
ssd.does: Stores the system and files for good
ssd.ask: What does the M.2 SSD do?

motherboard.name: Motherboard
motherboard.text: A compact board for a slim case: the CPU (usually soldered), memory slots, M.2 and ports. Unplug every cable and undo its screws.
motherboard.does: Carries the CPU and links every part

power_board.name: Power board
power_board.text: It turns 230 V from the socket into the DC voltages for the board and the screen backlight. Its capacitors can stay charged: do not touch them.
power_board.does: Turns mains power into DC voltages
power_board.ask: What does the power board do?

printer_3d.title: Taking a 3D printer apart
printer_3d.intro: An FDM printer melts plastic filament and builds the object layer by layer. Before taking it apart, switch it off and let the nozzle and bed cool: they reach 200 °C.

extruder.name: Extruder and nozzle
extruder.text: Gears push the filament into the hot nozzle, where it melts at 200 °C and comes out as a 0.4 mm line. A fan cools each new layer at once.
extruder.does: Melts the plastic and lays it down in a thin line
extruder.ask: What does the extruder and nozzle do?

heated_bed.name: Heated bed
heated_bed.text: The flat plate the object is printed on heats to 60 °C so the first layer sticks and the part does not warp. Undo its four levelling wheels and unplug its cable.
heated_bed.does: Holds the first layer down and stops warping
heated_bed.ask: What does the heated bed do?

steppers.name: Stepper motors
steppers.text: Four motors (X, Y, Z and extruder) turn in exact 1.8° steps, so the head and bed move to within hundredths of a millimetre.
steppers.does: Move the head and bed in exact steps
steppers.ask: What does the stepper motors do?

belts.name: Belts and lead screw
belts.text: Toothed belts turn the motors’ rotation into X and Y travel; the Z lead screw lifts the head for each layer.
belts.does: Turn motor rotation into straight motion
belts.ask: What does the belts and lead screw do?

control_board.name: Control board
control_board.text: A microcontroller reads the G-code line by line, sends step pulses to the motors and holds the nozzle and bed temperatures.
control_board.does: Reads the G-code and drives the motors and heaters
control_board.ask: What does the control board do?

psu.name: Power supply
psu.text: It turns 230 V into 24 V DC for the motors and heaters (up to 350 W). Unplug it and wait a few minutes before disconnecting it.
psu.does: Supplies 24 V to the motors and heaters
psu.ask: What does the power supply do?
